messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis
Details:
The failing test case calls WordUtils.abbreviate with parameters where the lower bound (15) is greater than the length of the string ("0123456789" length 10).

Inspecting the method abbreviate(String str, int lower, int upper, String appendToEnd) shows the following parameter adjustments:
- If upper is -1 or greater than str.length(), upper is set to str.length() (lines 618-620).
- Then if upper < lower, upper is set to lower (lines 621-623).

However, there is no equivalent adjustment for the lower parameter itself to ensure it is never greater than str.length().

This leads to a condition where:
- lower is greater than str.length(),
- upper is adjusted to at least lower (hence also greater than str.length()),
- then later calls str.substring(0, upper) (line 629 or 635) throw a StringIndexOutOfBoundsException because upper is beyond the string length.

The existing comments on lines 614-621 confirm the intended logic mentions adjusting lower to str.length() if it is greater. But the implementation lacks that step, causing the observed error.

Therefore, the root cause is the missing adjustment of lower to the string length, allowing upper to become out of bounds, causing substring calls to fail.

This matches the current bug report exactly:
- It describes the problem with upper adjusted to lower but lower not adjusted to string length,
- Resulting in upper > str.length(),
- Causing StringIndexOutOfBoundsException.

Recent unrelated bug reports do not impact this diagnosis.

The fix would be to add a check early in the method to adjust lower to str.length() if lower > str.length() before adjusting upper.

This explains the failed test and the exception encountered.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
